items.summary: Portées par la demande due à la guerre en Ukraine, les usines slovaques de fabrication d’obus tournent à plein régime. Notamment celles du groupe tchèque CSG, devenu un colosse européen de l’industrie de la défense.

items.title: Italie, Belgique, Espagne, Portugal : en Europe, la colère sociale gagne du terrain, sur fond de flambée des prix de l’énergie et de crise du logement
items.summary: Le coût de la vie et les conséquences de la hausse du prix de l’énergie mobilisent ailleurs qu’en France. Les images de manifestations, parfois violentes, se multiplient à travers l’Europe. Les Italiens sont appelés à une grève générale le 20 novembre, tandis qu’un mouvement similaire est prévu pour le 11 novembre en Espagne et au Portugal.

Planetary 'twins' Uranus and Neptune may have different origin stories
items.summary: By indirectly probing the depths of Uranus and Neptune's atmospheres, an international team of scientists has revealed a significant contrast in their chemical composition. Neptune appears to be more enriched in oxygen than Uranus. These results suggest that the two ice giants may have formed in different regions of the primitive solar system before reaching their current orbits, calling into question the idea of a common origin for these two planets, often considered twins.

items.title: [Perspectives] Shadows and interiority
items.summary: American television series The Pitt may have redefined the popularity of medical drama, but hospitals have always provided a rich seam for creatives, whether their medium is page or screen. From novels like Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn's 1966 Soviet-era Cancer Ward and Abraham Verghese's epic saga Cutting for Stone (2009) all the way through to television dramas such as Casualty, ER, and Grey's Anatomy, it seems we can’t get enough of human stories played out in a tense clinical setting. This is the absolute opposite of what author Chloe Aridjis does in The Shadow of the Object.

items.title: [Perspectives] Beyond the battlefield: war and global health security
items.summary: During the Syrian war (2011–24), the Assad Government forces and their Russian allies conducted hundreds of strikes on medical facilities in opposition-held areas. Monitoring groups documented over 600 attacks on health care, resulting in the deaths of hundreds of health-care workers throughout the conflict. Hospitals in eastern Aleppo and other contested regions were reduced to rubble. Surgeons operated in underground rooms illuminated by generators, and ambulances were targeted while transporting patients between sites.

items.title: [Perspectives] Temporal rationing: a man with gastric cancer in Colombia
items.summary: Pepe, a 45-year-old man living in the city of Cali, Colombia, worked as a self-employed hauler of goods with a wheelbarrow. In 2010, he presented to a general practitioner with several months of abdominal heaviness and non-exertional substernal burning. The physician provisionally diagnosed gastro-oesophageal reflux disease and prescribed omeprazole. However, Pepe's symptoms slowly worsened and 10 weeks later he returned to the physician, who ordered a gastroscopy, which occurred 2 months later, revealing an ulcerated mass.

items.title: [Editorial] Rethinking threats to human survival
items.summary: Much health advocacy is driven by single-issue activism. Communities with a common interest—from AIDS to child health, climate to tobacco control—focus intensely on their own domain. And understandably so. Important progress has been made through often courageous direct action. But this sharply competitive approach is, according to a new Lancet Commission on 21st Century Global Threats to Health, dangerously flawed. Indeed, perhaps the most important contribution of this Commission is to move global health beyond the consideration of individual harms.

items.summary: It is a general observation that the degree of weight loss obtained with GLP-1 receptor agonists is less in individuals with type 2 diabetes than in people without diabetes and similar BMI.
